summary: Children aged 5–6 read and draw o'clock and half-past times on an analogue clock. The crux is that the two hands measure different things and move together: at half past, the minute hand points to the 6 and the hour hand sits HALFWAY between two numbers. The time is read as 'half past the last number the hour hand has passed' — not the number it is nearest. Establish o'clock first, then half past, pairing reading with drawing in both directions.
misconceptions: Puts or expects the hour hand exactly on a number at half past, instead of halfway between
Confuses the minute and hour hands (reads or draws the wrong one)
Reads half past by the number the hour hand is nearest rather than the one it has passed (half past 3 read as half past 4)
Reads the clock as a bare number, matching a hand to a numeral, ignoring what each hand measures

activities.title: Wind the clock and watch the hour hand slide
steps: On a geared teaching clock (one where turning the minute hand drives the hour hand in proportion), start at 7 o'clock with the minute hand on 12 and the hour hand exactly on the 7.
Slowly turn the minute hand clockwise (the way clock hands normally go: 12, 1, 2, 3…) round the face to the 6, and watch the hour hand crawl away from the 7 toward the 8.
Stop when the minute hand reaches the 6 — half a turn round — and check where the hour hand is: it sits exactly halfway between 7 and 8.
Say the time aloud as 'half past 7', naming which hand told you it was a HALF (the minute hand, half way round) and which told you the hour (the hour hand, past the 7).
Repeat starting from several other o'clock positions (3, 9, 11) so you see the same halfway pattern each time.
activities.insight: At half past, the hour hand is dragged halfway between two numbers by the minute hand's half turn; 'half past 7' means 'half way past 7', not 'hour hand on 7 or 8'.

activities.title: Name each hand before you read
steps: Look at a clock where the short hand (hour) and long hand (minute) are colour-coded differently.
Before saying any time, point to each hand and say its job: 'short hand = the hour', 'long hand = the minutes'.
Read several clocks (e.g. 3 o'clock, half past 9) always naming the hand first, then the time.
Deliberately spot a swapped reading: if someone treated the long (minute) hand as if it gave the hour, explain why that reading would be wrong.
activities.insight: The two hands measure different quantities; reading a clock means interpreting what each hand tells you, not matching a hand to the nearest numeral.

activities.title: Draw the hands to show a time
steps: On a blank clock face, draw both hands for a given o'clock time (e.g. 3 o'clock): long minute hand on 12, short hour hand exactly on the 3.
On a fresh blank face, draw half past 7: minute hand on 6, and the hour hand drawn HALFWAY between the 7 and the 8.
Check your own drawing by asking: has the hour hand passed the 7 but not reached the 8? Is the minute hand on the 6?
Explain in words why the hour hand is between the numbers and not on one.
Try several more (half past 9, half past 11) and each time place the hour hand between the two numbers.
activities.insight: Showing a time requires constructing both hands correctly — especially placing the hour hand between numbers for half past — which asks more of the child than recognising a correct clock.

activities.title: Which hour has it passed? (reasoning the half-past hour)
steps: Look at a clock with the minute hand on 6 and the hour hand between two numbers (e.g. between 3 and 4).
Decide whether it is half past 3 or half past 4, and state the rule you used.
Trace which number the hour hand has already LEFT and which it is heading toward.
Respond to the claim 'It is half past 11, so the hour hand should point to 11' — explain why that is wrong and where the hour hand really goes.
Link to halves: the minute hand has travelled half way round the face, which is why we say 'half' past.
activities.insight: At half past you name the hour by the last number the hour hand has passed, not the number it is nearest or heading toward.

checkQuestion: Interpret, then translate. (Interpret) Show a clock reading half past 3 — minute hand on 6, hour hand halfway between 3 and 4: 'What time is this? How do you know — what is each hand telling you?' (Translate) Give a blank clock face: 'Now draw the hands to show half past 7.'
checkAnswer: Reads 'half past 3', explaining the minute hand on 6 means half way round (half past) and the hour hand between 3 and 4 means it is past 3 (the last number passed). Draws half past 7 with the minute hand on 6 and the hour hand HALFWAY between 7 and 8.
